stem: A 56-year-old woman comes to the office due to a persistent dry cough for the last month.  She has no fever, chest pain, or shortness of breath.  Medical history includes diabetes mellitus and a myocardial infarction 2 months ago.  She has never smoked.  Blood pressure is 130/70 mm Hg and pulse is 70/min.  The lungs are clear to auscultation.  Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in evaluating this patient?​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌​​‌‌​​​​​‌‌‌‌​‌​​​​‌‌​‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​​​‌​​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​​​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​​‌​​​​‌​​​‌​​​‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​​​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌​​​‌​​‌​​​​‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​‌‌​‌​​‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​​​‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌​‌​‌​​​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​​​‌​​​‌​​​​‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​​​‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌​​‌‌​‌​​​‌​​‌‌​‌‌​​​​​​‌‌​​​‌‌​​​​‌
explanation:
This patient with diabetes mellitus and a recent myocardial infarction is likely taking an ACE inhibitor (eg, lisinopril, ramipril), as these drugs are indicated to reduce cardiac remodeling following myocardial infarction and help slow the progression of diabetic kidney disease.  A persistent dry cough is one of the most common adverse effects of ACE inhibitors (~10% of patients).

ACE converts angiotensin I to angiotensin II and also degrades bradykinin and substance P.  ACE inhibition allows these mediators to accumulate, which can sensitize airway sensory nerves and increase the cough reflex.

Due to the widespread use of ACE inhibitors, an ACE inhibitor-induced cough should be one of the first considerations in patients presenting with persistent cough.  Because angiotensin II receptor blockers (eg, losartan) do not inhibit ACE activity, they are unlikely to cause a cough and are often an optimal replacement medication.

(Choices A, C, and E)  Other common causes of chronic cough include asthma, gastroesophageal reflux disease, and allergic rhinitis (ie, postnasal drip).  Asthma typically causes episodic wheezing and dyspnea and can be evaluated with pulmonary function testing; however, cough may occasionally be its only manifestation.  Given this patient's recent myocardial infarction, possible ACE inhibitor use, and absence of typical asthma symptoms, medication review is the most appropriate next step.  Allergy history and pulmonary function testing may guide further evaluation if medication review does not identify a likely cause.  Family history is less likely to explain the new cough.

(Choice B)  Chest x-ray can identify pulmonary causes of cough, including infection, malignancy, and pulmonary edema.  Although appropriate for patients with an unexplained chronic cough or in those with concerning clinical findings (eg, fever, hemoptysis), it does not replace medication review as the next step in this otherwise stable patient with possible ACE inhibitor exposure.

Educational objective:ACE inhibitors can cause a persistent dry cough, likely due to accumulation of bradykinin and substance P.  Medication review is an essential early step in evaluating persistent cough.  When ACE inhibitor–induced cough is suspected, the drug should be discontinued; an angiotensin II receptor blocker can often be substituted because it does not inhibit degradation of these mediators.​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌​​‌‌​​​​​‌‌‌‌​‌​​​​‌‌​‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​​​‌​​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​​​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​​‌​​​​‌​​​‌​​​‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​​​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌​​​‌​​‌​​​​‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​‌‌​‌​​‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​​​‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌​‌​‌​​​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​​​‌​​​‌​​​​‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​​​‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌​​‌‌​‌​​​‌​​‌‌​‌‌​​​​​​‌‌​​​‌‌​​​​‌
